_readme: Raw JSON-RPC captured by speaking the protocol directly over the claims-system server's stdin/stdout — no mcp SDK client involved in this capture, only subprocess pipes, so every field below is exactly what crossed the wire. The 'request'/'response' objects are untouched; '_annotations' is hand-written commentary added alongside, never inside, the raw messages. Captured by /private/tmp/.../scratchpad/capture_wire.py, reproducible against src/mcp_servers/claims_system_server.py.

_annotations.jsonrpc: Protocol version tag JSON-RPC 2.0 itself requires on every message — present on both request and response, always this literal string.
_annotations.id: Client-chosen correlation id (here: 1). The server echoes it back on the matching response so an async client can match replies to requests out of order — irrelevant over stdio with one request in flight at a time, but the wire format doesn't know that.
_annotations.method (request): 'initialize' — the mandatory first call of any MCP session. Nothing else may be sent before this.
_annotations.params.protocolVersion: The MCP spec version the client speaks (2024-11-05 here). The server can refuse an incompatible version — it didn't need to.
_annotations.params.capabilities (request): What the CLIENT supports (empty here — this capture client declares none). In a real client this would list e.g. sampling support.
_annotations.params.clientInfo: Free-text client identity for logging/debugging on the server side — not used for authorization.
_annotations.result.protocolVersion (response): The server confirming it will speak the same version back.
_annotations.result.capabilities (response): What the SERVER supports: logging, prompts, resources, and tools (listChanged: true — meaning it will tell a subscribed client if its tool list changes at runtime). This server exposes tools only, hence prompts/resources report as present-but-empty capabilities.
_annotations.result.serverInfo: Which server answered, and its version — 'claims-system', fastmcp 4.0.5. This is the field that would tell an auditor which of the two servers a given wire log came from.

_annotations.jsonrpc/method: A NOTIFICATION, not a request — note there is no 'id' field at all. JSON-RPC notifications never get a response; this is the client's one-way signal 'handshake complete, I'm ready for real calls now'.
_annotations.params: Empty — this notification carries no payload, it is purely a state transition.
_annotations.response: null, by design — a notification is fire-and-forget. This row exists in this capture only to document that fact, not because a response was expected and missing.

_annotations.id: 2 — a fresh correlation id, independent of the initialize call's id=1.
_annotations.method: 'tools/list' — this is THE discovery call requirement 1/3 depend on: the client asks 'what can you do', the server answers with real schemas, and nothing about which specific tools exist is hardcoded on either side.
_annotations.params: Empty here; a real client could page a very long tool list via a cursor param — this server has only two tools, no paging needed.
_annotations.result.tools[].name: The literal string the model must send back on Action/tools-call — 'get_claim_status', 'get_adjuster_notes'.
_annotations.result.tools[].description: THIS is the docstring-as-prompt, verbatim. 'Get claim status.' / 'Get adjuster notes.' — both deliberately bad right now, on purpose, to capture the BEFORE state for error_before_after.md; see that file for the improved version and what changed once it was rewritten.
_annotations.result.tools[].inputSchema: JSON Schema the client must satisfy — claim_number is a required string, additionalProperties:false means an extra/misspelled argument is rejected before the tool body even runs.
_annotations.result.tools[].outputSchema: Declared as an open object (additionalProperties:true) — fastmcp inferred this from the Python return type (a plain dict), not hand-written.
_annotations.result.tools[]._meta: fastmcp's own bookkeeping (tags, etc.) — not part of the core MCP spec, safe for a client to ignore.

_annotations.id: 3 — the third and last correlation id used in this capture.
_annotations.method: 'tools/call' — the only message type that actually executes application code. Everything before this was pure discovery/metadata; this is the one line in the whole exchange where the claims_store lookup for C-001 actually ran.
_annotations.params.name: Which discovered tool to invoke — 'get_claim_status', copied verbatim from tools/list's result.tools[].name; the client never invents this string.
_annotations.params.arguments: The claim_number argument, validated against the inputSchema from step 3 before the tool body ran (a malformed argument would fail here, before touching claims_store.py at all).
_annotations.result.content: A list of content blocks — here one TextContent block whose .text is the tool's return value, JSON-encoded as a string. This is what a client reads to get the answer.
_annotations.result.isError: false — this specific call succeeded. See error_before_after.md for what this same field looks like on a failing claim_number, before and after the error-message rewrite.
_annotations.result.structuredContent: The SAME data as result.content[0].text, but already parsed into a real JSON object instead of a string — a newer MCP convenience so a client doesn't have to re-parse text it already has structured. Both fields always carry the same information here; a client can use either.

_where_the_model_runs: In none of the four exchanges above. Every message here is the client (a plain Python subprocess-pipe script, not an agent) talking JSON-RPC to the claims-system SERVER process — no LLM, no prompt, no API key exists on either side of this exchange. The one and only place an LLM is called anywhere in this system is inside src/agent/mcp_agent.py's ReAct loop, one layer above this file entirely, when it calls usage.call_llm() to decide WHICH of these already-discovered tools to invoke and with what arguments — a decision this wire capture has no part in making.
